units.t: Words Named After People.
Part one. The earl and the sandwich.
Some of the most ordinary words in English are actually people.
Real people, with real lives, whose names escaped and became part of the language.
A word that comes from a person's name is called an eponym, and in this lesson, we'll meet five of them.
Let's begin with lunch.
Sandwich.
S, A, N, D, W, I, C, H.
Here's an everyday example.
I grabbed a ham and cheese sandwich from the bakery on the way to work.
The sandwich is named after John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, an English aristocrat who lived in the 1700s.
Sandwich itself is a small town in Kent, in the south east of England, so strictly speaking, your lunch is named after a place by way of a person.
Nobody believes the earl invented the idea of putting food between bread.
People had been doing that for a very long time.
What he did was make it fashionable, and give it a name.
The famous story comes from a French travel writer called Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in the 1760s.
He reported that a government minister once spent twenty-four hours at a gambling table.
The minister was so absorbed in the game, Grosley wrote, that he ate nothing but some beef between slices of toasted bread.
This new snack, Grosley said, was named after the minister who invented it.
It's a great story, but it may not be fair.
The earl's modern biographer, the naval historian Nicholas Rodger, points out that Montagu was a hardworking official.
He suggests the earl was just as likely to have eaten his bread and beef at his desk, working late.
Either way, the word was already in use by 1762.
That year, the historian Edward Gibbon wrote in his journal about a London club he'd visited.
He saw some of the most important men in the country there, eating, in his words, a bit of cold meat, or a Sandwich.
So a busy aristocrat who didn't want to put down his cards, or his paperwork, gave the world its favourite lunch.
And a word he couldn't possibly have predicted.
Part two. A boycott and a cardigan.
Our second word has a much less cheerful story.
Boycott.
B, O, Y, C, O, T, T.
For example, the whole netball club decided to boycott the café after it doubled its prices.
Charles Boycott was a retired British army captain.
In 1880, he was working in County Mayo, in the west of Ireland, as a land agent for an absentee landlord.
His job was to manage the estate and collect rent from the tenant farmers.
Times were hard, harvests had been poor, and Irish tenants were organising to demand lower rents and fairer treatment.
The Irish nationalist leader Charles Stewart Parnell had recently suggested a new tactic.
Rather than using violence against a landlord or agent who treated tenants unfairly, the community could simply shun him.
When Boycott refused the tenants' demands and moved to evict some of them, that's exactly what happened.
His farm workers walked off the job.
Local shops wouldn't serve him.
The blacksmith wouldn't shoe his horses, and even the postman stopped delivering his mail.
His crops were left standing in the fields.
In the end, a group of volunteers was brought in from the north of Ireland to bring in the harvest.
They were guarded by around a thousand soldiers and police.
By most accounts, the whole operation cost many times more than the crops were worth.
Boycott left Ireland before the year was out.
But his name stayed behind.
Within weeks, newspapers were using boycott as a verb, and it quickly spread well beyond English.
A version of the word is now used in French, German, Dutch and many other languages.
Our third word takes us to a battlefield.
Cardigan.
C, A, R, D, I, G, A, N.
For example, take a cardigan, it gets cold on the ferry once the sun goes down.
James Brudenell, the seventh Earl of Cardigan, was a wealthy British cavalry officer with a reputation for being arrogant and quarrelsome.
In October 1854, during the Crimean War, he led the Charge of the Light Brigade at the Battle of Balaclava.
Because of a confused order, hundreds of cavalrymen rode straight down a valley towards Russian guns.
Many were killed or wounded, but the earl survived and came home a celebrity.
The poet Alfred Tennyson turned the disaster into one of the most famous poems in English, with its line, into the valley of Death rode the six hundred.
The charge was a military blunder, but back in Britain it was celebrated as an example of courage and duty.
The knitted woollen waistcoat that he and his officers wore to keep warm became fashionable, and it took his name.
That same war gave us two more clothing words.
The raglan sleeve is named after Lord Raglan, the British commander.
And the balaclava is named after the battle itself, though that one's a place, not a person.
Part three. Shadows and trapezes.
Our fourth word is silhouette.
S, I, L, H, O, U, E, T, T, E.
For example, we sat on the beach and watched the silhouettes of surfers against the sunset.
Étienne de Silhouette was a French finance minister under King Louis the fifteenth.
He took the job in 1759, when France was deep in debt from war.
He tried to fix the problem with strict savings and new taxes, including taxes aimed at the rich.
It didn't go down well, and he lasted only about eight months.
His name, though, became a joke.
Doing something à la Silhouette came to mean doing it on the cheap.
At the time, a popular and inexpensive way to get a portrait was to trace someone's shadow and cut the outline from black paper.
These cheap shadow portraits got his name.
There's another theory too.
Silhouette was said to have enjoyed cutting out paper profiles himself as a hobby, and to have decorated his château with them.
Historians aren't sure which explanation is right, and it may be a bit of both.
Our fifth and final word is leotard.
L, E, O, T, A, R, D.
For example, my niece refuses to wear anything except her sparkly gymnastics leotard.
Jules Léotard was a French acrobat, and in 1859, in Paris, he performed what is often described as the first flying trapeze act.
He swung from one bar to another high above the audience, and he became a sensation.
He was only in his early twenties at the time.
He practised, the story goes, above the swimming pool his father ran in Toulouse, which would have made the falls a lot softer.
A popular song, The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze, was written about him.
Léotard wore a tight, one-piece outfit that let him move freely and show off his muscles.
He called it a maillot, but after his early death, it became known by his name.
So what should we take from all this?
First, eponyms are everywhere once you start listening for them.
The diesel engine is named after the German engineer Rudolf Diesel.
The saxophone is named after its Belgian inventor, Adolphe Sax.
Nicotine takes its name from Jean Nicot, a French diplomat who sent tobacco plants back to Paris in the 1500s.
Even the humble biro, as Australians call a ballpoint pen, is named after László Bíró, the Hungarian journalist who helped invent it.
Second, eponyms remind us that language isn't built only by scholars.
It's built by gossip, headlines and fashion.
A gambling story, a village protest, a war hero's jumper, a failed minister and a circus star all made it into everyday English.
To sum up, sandwich, boycott, cardigan, silhouette and leotard are all named after real people.
Some were honoured by their words, like Léotard, and some were mocked, like Silhouette.
Next time you pull on a cardigan or make a sandwich, you'll know who you're carrying with you.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which word comes from an Irish land agent who was shunned by his whole community in 1880?
Answer. Boycott, from Captain Charles Boycott.
Question two. The cardigan is named after an earl who led a famous cavalry charge. Which charge?
Answer. The Charge of the Light Brigade, in the Crimean War.
Question three. Why did the name of a French finance minister come to mean a cheap shadow portrait?
Answer. His penny-pinching made his name a byword for doing things on the cheap.
That's the end of Words Named After People. Catch you next time.
